sources.citation: Ethnologue 22nd ed. (2019), entry bsl Basa-Gumna (the Internet Archive 20190704010106).
sources.note: 'No known L1 speakers. The last fluent speaker shifted to Hausa [hau] by 1987.' Status 10 (Extinct). No resources listed.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. & Stuart McGill. 2012. The Kainji languages of Northwestern and Central Nigeria. Circulation draft, 11 May 2012, 369 pp. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation (Internet Archive copy of rogerblench.info PDF).
sources.note: Sec. 3.4 p. 13: Gumna deserted c. 1963, people at Yakila; 'In Yakila in 1986, there were only two people who spoke Basa, and that not well, so it is effectively dead.' Sec. 4.4 Basa-cluster phonology (p. 32) is an empty placeholder; all Basa-Gumna rows in the comparative wordlist appendix are blank; 'stress' occurs nowhere in the 369 pp.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. c. 2012. The Basa languages (web page, rogerblench.info Kainji/Basa/BasaOP.htm; Internet Archive copy).
sources.note: Classification list of seven Basa lects; no Basa-Gumna document linked; the Internet Archive's index of the site shows no Basa-Gumna wordlist was ever posted.

sources.citation: Johnston, Harry H. 1919. A comparative study of the Bantu and Semi-Bantu languages. Vol. I. Oxford: Clarendon Press. Group H 'The Central Nigerian languages': Semi-Bantu no. 256 'Basa' (with 254 Gurmana, 255 Kamuku); Basa vocabulary taken from Koelle 1854, Polyglotta Africana.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone for no. 256. The entry is a vocabulary column (nouns with singular/plural prefixes, numerals, pronouns) in the comparative tables plus a pooled prefix list for 254-256 ending 'Concord particles are present in Gurmana, Kamuku, and Basa, but their forms are little known.' Koelle-derived forms carry Koelle's acute accents (e.g. 'Bása') but Johnston makes no prosodic statement about this language; his only tone/accent remarks in vol. I are the general reader's notes (penultimate accent as the Bantu norm; acute/grave for high/low tone, 'in the case of the southern Nigeria…

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid basa1280 (page, JSON) and reference records 79196, 99051, 66310, 115581, 306337.
sources.note: Only two references for the language, both Glottolog's most extensive description 'a wordlist or less': Rowlands 1962 (short 'Kuta' word list; language code 'Bassa-Kuta from Kagara = [bsl]') and Gunn & Conant 1960 (ethnography). No grammar, sketch or phonology exists in Glottolog.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Basa-Gumna language' (stub).
sources.note: Cites only Ethnologue, Glottolog, Multitree and Blench 2012; nothing linguistic.

sources.citation: OLAC: 'OLAC resources in and about the Basa-Gumna language' (ISO 639-3 bsl), combined catalog page, up-to-date as of 2024-12-04 (Internet Archive capture).
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: No phonology content: the listing holds exactly two records, Glottolog 5.0 'Resources for Basa-Gumna' and Ethnologue 2018 'Basa-Gumna: a language of Nigeria'. No archive deposit, wordlist or recording for bsl in any OLAC archive.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2020 [ed. IV, 2019]. An Atlas of Nigerian Languages. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. Entry 39 Basa-Gumna–Basa-Kontagora cluster.
sources.note: Entry 39 '*Basa-Gumna [†]': alt. names Gwadara-Basa, Basa Kuta, Basa-Kaduna; Niger State, Chanchaga LGA; 'Only 2 known semi-speakers in 1987.. Probably now extinct. Source(s) Blench (1987)'; sec. 4.1: 'Basa-Gumna, a Basa lect, no competent speakers in 1987'. No linguistic description, nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2018. Nominal affixing in the Kainji languages of northwestern and central Nigeria. In J. R. Watters (ed.), East Benue-Congo: Nouns, pronouns, and verbs, 59-106. Berlin: Language Science Press.
sources.note: Table 25 p. 96 lists Basa-Gumna as extinct; p. 96 'for other languages in the cluster only wordlist data exists'; p. 97 'Tones were not marked when this data was collected' (Basa-Benue data). Nothing on stress for any Basa lect.

sources.citation: McGill, Stuart & Roger Blench. 2012. Documentation, development, and ideology in the northwestern Kainji languages. Language Documentation and Description 11: 90-135.
sources.note: Table 3 p. 99: '(Basa-Gumna)† — Interview with last rememberer (Blench 1976)'; p. 100: Basa-Gumna among Kainji languages that 'have become moribund.. without ever being described, let alone documented'. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Osaji, Bede. 1979. Language survey in Nigeria (Publication B-81). Quebec: International Center for Research on Bilingualism, Laval University. 180 pp. (ERIC ED 179 113 microfiche; archive.org item micro_IA41155110_0593). Entries 'Bassa-Kaduna'.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Nothing. A name/location/classification index compiled from Hansford et al. 1976 and similar lists: 'Bassa-Kaduna / Niger State, Minna Division / Benue-Congo: Wester Plateau: Kamuku-Bassa group' (the scanned text); alternate-name table 'Bassa-Kaduna / Gwandara-Bassa, / Bassa Kuta' (lines 6475-6477); listed among Niger State languages (line 16619). The words stress/tone/accent occur only in non-linguistic or Hausa-dialect contexts elsewhere in the document.

sources.citation: Meek, C. K. 1925. The Northern Tribes of Nigeria: an ethnographical account of the Northern Provinces of Nigeria together with a report on the 1921 decennial census. Vol. II. London: Oxford University Press (Humphrey Milford). Chapter 'Language and Lore' (pp. c. 132-147).
sources.note: Classificatory language chapter built on government vocabularies (c. 1921): lists 'Basa (Kaduna)' under Nigerian Semi-Bantu; notes that in noun plural formation 'Basa, Gurmana, Kamuku, and Koro show a certain amount of resemblance' (p. 144); lists 'Basa (Kaduna)' among languages with gender distinction in 2nd and 3rd person pronouns and gives the form 'Basa has bua' (pp. 146-147). No phonology; the words stress/tone/accent do not occur in a linguistic sense anywhere in the volume.

sources.citation: Temple, O. (ed. C. L. Temple). 1922. Notes on the tribes, provinces, emirates and states of the Northern Provinces of Nigeria, compiled from official reports. 2nd ed. Lagos: C.M.S. Bookshop. Entry 'BASSA'.
sources.note: No phonology content. Only: 'In the Niger Province they speak a language which bears some affinity to Baushi. It is possible that the Kamberri, Dukawa, Baushi, Ura, Ngwoi, and Kamuku may be akin to the Bassa..' (the scanned text).

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 1976/1986. Basa-Gumna: interview with last rememberer / field notes (unpublished; cited as 'Blench 1976' in McGill & Blench 2012 Table 3 and 'Blench (1987)' in the Atlas of Nigerian Languages).

sources.note: The only first-hand linguistic record of Basa-Gumna; never published or posted (the Internet Archive's index shows no such file on rogerblench.info). Would be the only place any pronunciation/prosody note could exist.
